analysis.one_liner: Quadruples the excise tax on corporate stock buybacks, from 1% to 4%.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2023 with 10 Senate sponsors but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2023's Inflation Reduction Act, companies pay a 1% tax when they buy back their own stock. This bill would have raised that to 4%, making it costlier for corporations to repurchase shares, and it would have exempted stock given to executives from the offsetting adjustment so those grants count as real buybacks. It died in the Senate Finance Committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the federal government would have collected more revenue from corporations that repurchase stock, and companies would have faced a stronger incentive to reinvest in workers, wages, and equipment instead of buybacks. Ordinary taxpayers indirectly benefit when corporate profits are taxed rather than recycled into share-price support.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1% to 4%, applied to repurchases after enactment [S3].
The CRS summary confirms the sole purpose is increasing the buyback excise tax rate from 1% to 4% [S2].

The bill also changes the adjustment rules so that stock issued to 'covered employees' — the statute's term for top executives — no longer offsets a company's buyback tax bill, closing a way corporations could claw back the tax through executive stock grants [S3].
The bill had 10 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors, including the chairman of the Finance Committee, Senator Ron Wyden [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that buy back their own stock would pay four times the current tax, and their shareholders — concentrated among wealthy households and institutional investors — would bear the cost directly or through somewhat lower share-price support. Companies might also shift cash to dividends instead, which are taxed differently.

drawbacks.text: An excise tax on buybacks is a blunt instrument: companies can redirect the same cash to dividends, which shareholders may prefer anyway, limiting the tax's effect on behavior and the revenue it raises. This is a general policy-mechanism point about how buyback taxes work.

The tax's cost would be felt partly by retirement savers and ordinary investors through mutual funds and pensions that hold repurchasing companies' stock, since shareholders ultimately bear corporate taxes [S3].
Raising a tax enacted only in 2023, before its effects were well studied, makes it harder to judge whether 4% is the right rate or whether the tax is doing what supporters intend [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a simple, two-page rate increase on a tax that already existed, with a targeted fix so executive stock grants could not offset the tax. The main costs fall on corporations and their shareholders, including retirement accounts holding those shares, and some of the intended pressure on buybacks could leak into dividends instead. The public benefit — more corporate tax revenue and modest pressure to invest in operations rather than share prices — is real but moderate, not transformative.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on February 14, 2023, joined by six original cosponsors including Finance Chairman Ron Wyden, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance that same day [S3] [S5].
Nine additional senators cosponsored the bill, all Democrats [S4].

The action history shows no further activity after the referral to Finance: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that repurchase stock and their largest shareholders are better off, because the excise tax stayed at 1% instead of rising to 4%. The Finance Committee's failure to act spared those companies any increase, and no compensating revenue was raised.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but his committee never held a markup or moved it to the floor.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Republican Senate minority
against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and Republicans controlled the agenda-setting paths available for tax bills in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans joined, and the bill never advanced in the Finance Committee during divided government.
